1.pericope_label: The seven altars and the going aside

schools.summary: Gill notes that Balaam spoke when upon one of the high places of Baal, after having taken a view of the people of Israel as they lay encamped, and that Balak did as he had spoken, ordering seven altars to be built and seven bullocks and rams prepared. From the direction to stand by the burnt offering he infers that the sacrifices offered were of that sort, and that there might be one which was more peculiarly the burnt offering of Balak, though he might be more or less concerned in them all; at that offering he was directed to stand while it was burning. Calvin concludes from the manner of the proceeding that this degenerate prophet had by no means been wont to prophesy in accordance with pure revelations from God, but that the art of divination in which he boasted had some affinity to magical exorcisms and was infected with many errors and deceptions; this did not prevent him from being sometimes a true prophet, since it was God's will that some little sparks of light should still shine while the world was plunged in darkness, in order to render even the most ignorant inexcusable. Being endowed only with a special gift, Balaam borrowed devices in various directions which savoured of nothing but the illusions of the devil and were utterly foreign to the true and legitimate method of consulting God, and hence came the seven victims and the seven altars. God, by consecrating the seventh day to himself, and in the seven lamps and other things, had indicated that there was something of perfection in that number; but afterwards many strange superstitions were invented, and under this pretence Satan cunningly deluded wretched men by persuading them that secret virtues were contained in the number seven. The same frivolous subtlety prevailed among profane writers, who sought confirmation of the error throughout all nature, alleging the seven planets, as many Pleiades, and the seven stars of the Wain. In seeking retirement, he adds, Balaam imitates the true servants of God, since God has almost always appeared to his servants when they have been separated from the company of men; you would say that he was another Moses when he exhorts the king to persevering prayer and bids him stand by his offering that he may be more earnest in supplication.

Henry says great preparation was made for the cursing of Israel, the aim being to engage the God of Israel to forsake them and either take Moab's side or stand neuter, and exclaims at the sottishness of superstition which imagines that God will be at men's beck. Balaam and Balak think to bribe him with altars and sacrifices offered without any warrant or institution of his, as if he would eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats: ridiculous nonsense, to think that these would please God and gain his favour, when there could be in them no exercise either of faith or obedience. It should seem, he allows, that they offered these sacrifices to the God of heaven, the supreme Divinity, and not to any of their local deities; but the multiplying of altars was an instance of their degeneracy from the religion of their ancestors and their apostasy to idolatry, for those that multiplied altars multiplied gods, as Ephraim made many altars to sin. They liked not to retain God in their knowledge but became vain in their imaginations, and yet presumptuously expected to gain him over from Israel, who had his sanctuary among them and his anointed altar. He observes besides how very imperious Balaam was, proud to have the command of a king and to give law to princes, such being the spirit of that wicked one who exalts himself above all that is called God; with what authority he gives orders to build seven altars in the place he has pitched upon, covering his malice against Israel with a show of devotion, though his sacrifice was an abomination, being brought with such a wicked mind, since what he aimed at was not to honour God with the sacrifices of righteousness but to enrich himself with the wages of unrighteousness. And he observes how very obsequious Balak was.

Clarke's block on the first verse is an analysis of the chapter's course, that Balaam, having arrived at the high places of Baal, orders Balak to build seven altars and prepare oxen and rams for sacrifice, inquires of the Lord, receives an answer and returns with it to Balak, who is greatly troubled to find it a prediction of the prosperity of the Israelites. On the direction to stand by the burnt offering he says blessing and cursing in this way were considered as religious rites and therefore must always be preceded by sacrifice, as may be seen in the case of Isaac before he blessed Jacob and Esau. Wesley says the seven altars were built to the true God, since otherwise Balaam would not have mentioned them to God as an argument why he should grant his requests; and though Balak was averse from God and his worship, he would be easily overruled by Balaam, who doubtless told him that it was in vain to make an address to any other than the God of Israel. To stand by the burnt offering he takes as standing in God's presence, as one that offers himself as well as his sacrifices to obtain his favour; Balaam's going he takes of some solitary and convenient place where he might prevail with God to appear to him, and the showing as revealing either by word or sign. The high place he renders otherwise, saying that the word properly signifies the plain.

Ellicott observes that the patriarchs of old, and their pious descendants after the giving of the Law, never erected more than one altar in one place, so that a plurality of altars was the badge of idolatry; and he adduces Hengstenberg for several instances proving that the ancients were accustomed to have recourse to sacrifice and conjuration in order to avert calamity and produce prosperity, the number seven having been regarded as significant among the Greeks and Romans as well as among the Israelites. Of the offering he thinks it more probable that Balak, as a king, performed priestly functions than that Balaam performed them alone. The high place he renders rather as a bare or barren height, noting that the heathen augurs were accustomed to choose elevated places for their auspices with an extensive prospect, especially the barren summits of mountains. Keil's block on this span is chiefly verse quotation, marking only that what follows came after the offering of the sacrifices.

debates: To whom the sacrifices were offered and in what spirit: Wesley says plainly that the altars were built to the true God and that Balaam told Balak it was vain to address any other, while Henry allows the object but condemns the form, since those that multiplied altars multiplied gods, and Ellicott calls a plurality of altars the badge of idolatry outright

Where the sevens came from: Calvin traces them to a real divine indication of perfection in the number, afterwards corrupted by superstition and by Satan's persuasion that secret virtues lay in it, while Ellicott traces the significance of seven to the common practice of Greeks and Romans as well as Israelites

What Balaam was: Calvin holds that he was endowed only with a special gift and borrowed his devices from methods foreign to the legitimate consulting of God, yet imitates the true servants of God so closely that one would call him another Moses, while Henry sees only imperiousness and the wages of unrighteousness

Who performed the sacrifices: Ellicott thinks it more probable that Balak as king discharged priestly functions than that Balaam acted alone, while Gill supposes one offering peculiarly Balak's with the prophet concerned in them all

Whether Balaam went up or went out: Ellicott renders the place a bare or barren height, on the practice of heathen augurs seeking an extensive prospect, while Wesley says the word properly signifies the plain
outliers: Henry's exclamation at the sottishness of superstition which imagines that God will be at men's beck
Calvin's tracing of the seven-fold superstition through profane writers to the seven planets, the Pleiades and the stars of the Wain
Calvin's judgement that God let some sparks of light shine even through a corrupt prophet in order to render the most ignorant inexcusable
Ellicott's citation of Hengstenberg on sacrifice and conjuration used to avert calamity
Clarke's rule that blessing and cursing were religious rites which must be preceded by sacrifice, illustrated from Isaac and his sons
Henry's charge that Balaam's aim was not the sacrifices of righteousness but the wages of unrighteousness
Wesley's reading of the posture, that Balak offered himself as well as his sacrifices

4.pericope_label: God meets Balaam, and the first parable begins

schools.summary: Gill says God met Balaam not in a kind and gracious manner, not out of any respect to him and his offerings, not to indulge him with spiritual communion, nor to communicate his mind and will to him as to a friend, nor to gratify his desires. The Lord put a word in his mouth, he says, not grace into his heart nor the fear of God within him, but suggested to him what to say, impressed it so strongly upon him that he could not forget it and with such power and weight that he was obliged to deliver it; and he returned immediately, as soon as he was told what to say. The parable he calls the prophetic word which God had put into his mouth, so called because prophecies are often figurative and enigmatical, the Targums of Jonathan and Jerusalem calling it the parable of his prophecy. On the disclaimer he says the sense is that it was impossible for Balaam to curse those whom God did not curse himself or would not have cursed by others; not but that he had a good will to it, to get Balak's money and honour, but he knew it was in vain to attempt what could not possibly be done. God does not and will not curse his spiritual Israel, who are blessed in Christ and shall be blessed, nor is it in the power of their enemies to do them harm; and he notes that instead of God and the Lord in this and the following clause the Targums use the phrase the Word of the Lord, the essential Word, the Son of God, who is so far from cursing his people that he has delivered them from the curses of the law, being made a curse for them. Calvin says it is wonderful that God should have determined to have anything in common with the pollutions of Balaam, since there is no communion between light and darkness and he detests all association with demons; but however hateful the impiety of Balaam was, God made use of him in this particular act. This was by no means a proof of his favour, as if he approved of the seven altars and sanctioned these superstitions, but as he well knows how to apply corrupt instruments to his use, so by the mouth of this false prophet he promulgated the covenant which he had made with Abraham to foreign and heathen nations. Balaam boasts of his seven altars as if he had duly propitiated God, and thus do hypocrites arrogantly trust that they deserve well of God when they do but provoke his anger; God, however, passes over this corrupt worship and proceeds with what he had determined, sending Balaam to be a proclaimer and witness of the sureness of his grace towards his chosen people. He supplies his servants with what they speak and controls their tongues, for neither would they be sufficient to think anything unless the ability were bestowed by him, and no one can say that Jesus is the Lord but by the Holy Ghost; still the holy prophets were in such wise organs of the Spirit that they gave forth from the heart the treasures which God had deposited with them, as Jeremiah says that he did eat the words of God and Ezekiel that he ate the roll on which his prophecies were written, for we must not conceive an inspiration such as that by which the heathens supposed their diviners to be carried away and thrown into ecstasy. The word rendered parable, he adds, signifies all weighty and notable sayings, especially when expressed in exalted language, so that the meaning is that Balaam began to speak eloquently and in no ordinary strain, arousing Balak's attention by a secret influence, that the wretched man might acknowledge there was something of divine inspiration in his words. The sum of the saying is that there was not merely perversity and folly in Balak's design, but that whatever he attempted would be vain, since he was fighting against God; and Balaam renounces for himself the power which Balak was persuaded he eminently possessed, since Balak had said that he knew whom Balaam cursed was cursed, as if the power of God were transferred to him to exercise according to his will, which was nothing but to depose God from his supremacy. Not that God always restrains the wicked from declaring what is opposed to his truth, for we know that they often prate at random, vomit forth their blasphemies by the mouthful and obscure the light by their falsehoods; but inasmuch as Balaam was compelled to play a different part, he confesses that his tongue was tied, so that he could not utter a single syllable against God's command.

Clarke refers the word rendered parable to his earlier note, and says that all these oracular speeches of Balaam are in hemistich metre in the original, that they are highly dignified, and that they may be considered as immediate poetic productions of the Spirit of God. On the disclaimer he says it was granted on all hands that no incantations nor imprecations could avail unless God concurred and ratified them, and that from God's communication to him Balaam saw that God was determined to bless and defend Israel. Wesley calls the parable Balaam's oracular and prophetical speech, so named because of the weightiness of the matter and the liveliness of the expressions which is usual in parables, and glosses Jacob as the posterity of Jacob.

Keil says God came to meet Balaam, who thought it necessary, as a true soothsayer, to call the attention of God to the altars he had built and the sacrifices offered upon them; God made known his will to him, though not in a natural sign of doubtful signification, putting a very distinct and unmistakeable word into his mouth and commanding him to make it known to the king. Of the opening of the parable he explains that Aram and the mountains of the east mean Mesopotamia, which was described as far back as Genesis as the land of the sons of the east, Balaam mentioning the mountains of his home. On the disclaimer he says Balak imagined, like all the heathen, that Balaam as a magician could dispense blessings and curses according to his own will and put such constraint upon his God as to make him subservient to that will, and that the seer opposes this delusion: the God of Israel does not curse his people, and therefore his servant cannot curse them, the verses that follow giving the reason. Ellicott quotes Bishop Wordsworth on the putting of the word into Balaam's mouth, that God, who had opened the mouth of the ass in a manner contrary to her nature, now opens Balaam's mouth in a manner contrary to his own will.

debates: Why God met Balaam at all: Gill denies every gracious construction of the meeting, Calvin calls it wonderful that God should have anything in common with such pollutions and explains it by his knowing how to apply corrupt instruments to his use, and Keil turns the boast about the altars into evidence that Balaam approached as a soothsayer expecting to attract God's notice

How the word came into Balaam's mouth: Gill distinguishes suggestion from grace in the heart, Ellicott quotes Wordsworth for the parallel with the ass's mouth opened contrary to nature, and Calvin uses the case to mark off true prophecy, in which the prophets gave forth from the heart what God had deposited with them, from the heathen ecstasy

What the word rendered parable means: Gill takes it of figurative and enigmatical speech, Wesley of weighty matter and lively expression, Calvin of any notable saying in exalted language, and Clarke of metre, holding the speeches to be immediate poetic productions of the Spirit of God

What Balaam's disclaimer concedes: Calvin makes it a renunciation of the very power Balak ascribed to him, which would have deposed God from his supremacy, while Keil makes it a refusal of the heathen assumption that a magician can constrain his God, and Clarke says all parties already granted that incantations avail only if God ratifies them

Whether God always restrains the wicked from speaking against his truth: Calvin denies it expressly, saying they often prate at random and vomit forth blasphemies, and confines the tying of the tongue to Balaam's particular case
outliers: Ellicott's citation of Bishop Wordsworth, that the mouth opened contrary to nature is matched by the mouth opened contrary to the man's own will
Calvin's rule that the prophets ate the words of God, as Jeremiah and Ezekiel say, and were not carried away as the heathen supposed of their diviners
Calvin's account of the hypocrite who trusts he deserves well of God at the very moment he provokes his anger
Clarke's metrical observation that the oracles are in hemistich metre in the original
Gill's note that the Targums replace God and the Lord with the Word of the Lord, whom he identifies with the Son who was made a curse for his people
Keil's phrase that God answered not by a natural sign of doubtful signification but by a distinct and unmistakeable word
Calvin's remark that by this false prophet's mouth the Abrahamic covenant was promulgated to heathen nations

9.pericope_label: The people that dwells alone, and the death of the righteous

schools.summary: Gill says Balaam was at this time on the top of a rock or high hill from which he had a view of Israel encamped in the plains of Moab below him. The dust of Jacob he takes of the people of Israel and their posterity, so called not because of their original, the dust of the earth, but because of their numbers, being as numerous as the dust of the earth or the sand of the sea, as it had been promised they should be. Balak's reproach he renders what hast thou done unto me, or for me, meaning nothing at all to answer his purpose or the end for which he had sent for him. Calvin holds that the meaning is that although Balaam only beheld the people from afar, so that he could not accurately perceive their power from so high and distant a spot, they still portended to him something great and formidable; a closer view generally intimidates men, and a body of twenty thousand men dazzles our sight as if the number were five times as great, whereas the real extent of a thing is more accurately ascertained at a distance. Balaam therefore declares, in the spirit of prophecy, that he sees far more in the people of God than their distance from him would allow, since, posted on a high eminence, he would have beheld them only as dwarfs with the ordinary vision of men. That the people shall dwell alone he takes as their being by no means in want of external support, so that they shall dwell content with their own condition, neither desiring the wealth or power of others nor seeking their aid; and the fact that the people had recourse at one time to the Egyptians and at another to the Assyrians, entangling themselves in improper alliances, is not repugnant to this prophecy, in which the question is not as to the virtue of the people but only as to the blessing of God, celebrated again in the same words in Deuteronomy. From the mention of the dust it is plain that what Balaam was to say was suggested to him by God, since he quotes the words of God's solemn promise wherein the seed of Abraham is compared to the dust of the earth; and although that multitude was reduced to a small number by the sin of the people, this was not declared in vain, inasmuch as that little body at length expanded itself so as to fill the whole world, their offspring being infinite since the fourth part is almost innumerable. The closing aspiration he calls more emphatic than a simple affirmation, since Balaam says he would that he might share with them their last end, for every one longs for what is most for his good, and Balaam confesses himself unworthy to be reckoned among them. Of Balak's reproach he says the proud man again reproaches the false prophet as if he had fairly purchased of him the right of prophecy and the authority to make him speak whatever he chose, and bids us behold how the reprobate seek God by crooked paths.

Henry says Balak was angry with Balaam, and that thus a confession of God's overruling power is extorted from a wicked prophet, to the confusion of a wicked prince. A second time the curse is turned into a blessing, and this blessing is both larger and stronger than the former; men change their minds, but God does not.

Clarke says the seeing was from the high places of Baal, where Balaam went that he might the more advantageously see the whole camp of Israel, and that the people shall dwell alone means they shall ever be preserved as a distinct nation, a prophecy he calls literally fulfilled. On the closing wish he departs from the received reading: it has been generally supposed that Balaam is here praying for a happy death, such as true Christians die who die in the Lord, and in this way his words are generally applied, but he is satisfied this is not their meaning. The death of the righteous in those times implied being gathered to one's fathers in a good old age, having seen his children and his children's children, and to this the latter part of the petition probably applies, the clause being better rendered let my posterity be like his; probably Balaam had some presentiment that he should be taken off by a premature death, and therefore lodges this petition against it. The prayer understood in the common way, he allows, is a good one and may be offered to God profitably, since a righteous man is one saved from his sins, justified and sanctified through the blood of the covenant, who lives not only an innocent but a holy and useful life, and he who would die well should live well. Wesley says the rocks are those upon which Balaam then stood, and that he sees the people according to Balak's desire but cannot improve that sight to the end for which it was designed, to curse them. The people shall dwell alone means that they are of a distinct kind from others, God's peculiar people; the dust means the numberless people of Jacob, who according to God's promise are now become as the dust of the earth; and the righteous he takes of this righteous and holy people, the sense being that they are not only happy above other nations in this life but hereafter.

Keil's blocks on this span are chiefly verse quotation, marking the two reasons why Balaam could not curse Israel and recording his answer, that he must take heed to speak that which the Lord had put in his mouth. Ellicott says that from the summit of the rocky mountain on which Balak had erected his seven altars Balaam had, according to one interpretation, a full view of the outstretched camps of Israel, and renders the clause better as, lo, it is a people that dwelleth alone and that is not numbered. In the fact that the host of Israel dwelt by itself in a separate encampment, he says, Balaam discerned a type of the essential separation of Israel from the surrounding nations, and when Israel adopted the ways of the heathen nations it speedily lost its external independence. On the last clause he quotes Hengstenberg, that how truly Balaam said Israel did not reckon itself with the heathen appears from the fact that while all the powerful empires of the ancient world, the Egyptian, Assyrian, Babylonian and others, have utterly perished, Israel, which even under the Old Covenant was rescued from so many dangers that threatened its entire destruction, particularly in being brought back from exile, flourishes anew in the Church of the New Covenant and continues also to exist in that part of it which, though at present rejected, is destined to restoration at a future period. The words about the dust of Jacob he refers back to the promise made to Abraham, that God would make his seed as the dust of the earth, and the fourth part of Israel to the four great encampments into which the Israelites were divided. Balak's complaint he renders from the Hebrew as thou hast blessed, to bless, an emphatic mode of stating that Balaam had continued to give utterance to nothing but blessings.

debates: What the wish to die the death of the righteous means: Clarke denies the received reading that Balaam prays for a happy death and renders the second clause let my posterity be like his, supposing a presentiment of premature death, Wesley refers the righteous to Israel as a people, and Calvin keeps the common sense while making the mood an aspiration in which Balaam confesses himself unworthy

What dwelling alone means: Clarke and Wesley take it of a distinct nation preserved as God's peculiar people, Ellicott of an essential separation lost whenever Israel adopted heathen ways, and Calvin of independence, a people content with their own condition and needing no external support
Whether Israel's later foreign alliances contradict the prophecy: Calvin raises the objection himself and answers that the question is not the virtue of the people but the blessing of God

How much Balaam could see from where he stood: Calvin argues that distance should have shown him dwarfs and that his seeing something great and formidable proves the spirit of prophecy, while Gill, Clarke and Ellicott treat the vantage point as simply affording a full view of the camp

What Balak's reproach assumes: Calvin says he reproaches the prophet as one from whom he had fairly purchased the right of prophecy, Ellicott renders the emphatic Hebrew as blessing to bless, and Henry makes the whole a confession extorted from a wicked prophet to the confusion of a wicked prince
outliers: Calvin's optical argument that twenty thousand men dazzle the sight at close quarters while distance shows a thing more truly
Ellicott's long quotation from Hengstenberg on Israel outliving Egypt, Assyria and Babylon and flourishing anew in the Church
Clarke's rendering of the second clause as let my posterity be like his, against the usual application of the verse to a happy death
Clarke's conjecture that Balaam had a presentiment of a premature death and prayed against it
Calvin's note that the multitude reduced by the people's sin at length expanded so as to fill the whole world
Henry's remark that men change their minds but God does not
Ellicott's explanation of the fourth part of Israel from the four great encampments

13.pericope_label: The second station, and Balak asks again what the Lord has said

schools.summary: Gill says Balak seemed satisfied with the answer, however, since he could not help himself and was willing to make the best of Balaam that he could and to try what he could do with him another time and elsewhere. The field of Zophim he explains as so called from the watch tower and the watchmen in it, reporting Jarchi that it was a high place where a watchman stood to observe if an army came against a city, and so a very proper place for the purpose. Of the repeated rites he notes only that Balak was to stand by his burnt offering as he had been directed before, and that the Lord met Balaam and put a word in his mouth as he had done before. On the second approach he observes from Jarchi that whereas the earlier verse says all the princes of Moab, this one does not, since when they saw there was no hope of succeeding some of them had withdrawn. Calvin says Balak did as almost all superstitious persons usually do, for since with them nothing is certain or established they are carried about from one speculation to another and try now this and now that expedient; and especially they imagine that there is some magical power in the sight, as if the eyes contributed partly to the efficacy of their incantations. It appears from profane writers that this was formerly a commonly received opinion, that the gaze of the enchanter had much effect upon his art, and Balak therefore removes his sorcerer to another place that there he might the better exercise his divinations. There is some ambiguity in the words, he adds, some rendering them as an invitation to see from thence, others as a warning that he shall see a part and not the whole, as if Balak feared that the multitude itself frightened Balaam or diminished the power of his incantations; and his block reports that Marckius concluded there is no sufficient reason for the proposed alteration of the Hebrew tense, since Balaam's earlier words about seeing from the top of the rocks are rather to be understood of a more complete than of an obscurer view. Of Balak's question he says he inquires what God had answered although he had rejected the previous revelation, and that thus do hypocrites profess anxious solicitude in inquiring the will of God whilst the knowledge of it is intolerable to them, so that their extreme earnestness in inquiring is of no value.

Henry says preparation was made the second time, as before, for the cursing of Israel, and that the place was changed because Balak fancied that Balaam, having so full a prospect of the whole camp from the top of the rocks, was either so enamoured with the beauty of it that he would not curse them or so affrighted with the terror of it that he durst not; therefore he would bring him to another place from which he might see only some part of them, which would appear more despicable, and that part at least which lay in view he hoped he might obtain leave to curse, so that by degrees he should get ground against them, intending no doubt, if he gained this point, to make his attack on that part of the camp which Balaam then had in his eye and into which he was to throw the fireballs of his curses. See, he says, how restless and unwearied the church's enemies are in their malicious attempts to ruin it: they leave no stone unturned, no project untried, to compass it; and O that we were as full of contrivance and resolution in prosecuting good designs for the glory of God. The sacrifices are then repeated, new altars built, a bullock and a ram offered on every altar, and Balak attends his sacrifice as closely as ever; and were we thus earnest to obtain the blessing as Balak was to procure a curse, designedly upon Israel but really upon himself, it would be well with us.

Clarke says Balak thought that the sight of such an immense camp had intimidated Balaam, and that he might gather this from what Balaam had said about the dust of Jacob, so that he supposed he might gain his point by removing him to another station. Of Balak's question he says Balak himself now understood that Balaam was wholly under the influence of Jehovah and would say nothing but what God commanded him, but that, not knowing Jehovah as Balaam did, he hoped that he might yet be induced to change his mind. Wesley says the meaning of the change of place is that Balak thought the sight of them all might discourage Balaam, or, as it had done before, raise his fancy to an admiration of the multitude and felicity of the people.

Ellicott says that if the received rendering of the clause about seeing the utmost part is correct, it strongly confirms the interpretation of the earlier verse according to which Balaam saw the whole host of Israel from the first station; the words may, however, be rendered as meaning that he sees here only the utmost part and does not see them all. If the interpretation of the earlier verse is adopted which restricts the view to the extremity of the host, the meaning would seem to be that if Balaam could obtain a full view of the entire army he would not only perceive the ground which existed for Balak's alarm but would be induced to put forth more strenuous efforts to deliver him from so formidable an invasion; if, on the other hand, that interpretation is adopted which implies that from the first station Balaam had a view of the whole host from one extremity of their camps to the other, the meaning would be that although the sight of so vast and orderly a mass produced so powerful an effect upon Balaam that he was unable to utter the curses he had desired to pronounce, such an effect would not follow a partial view. The field of Zophim he renders the field of watchers, and says the spot seems to be identified with that from which Moses afterwards surveyed the promised land, described as the mountain of Nebo, though it is possible that Pisgah may have had more than one such summit. On Balak's question he notes that he here speaks of God under the name Jehovah. Keil's blocks on this span are chiefly verse quotation, recording that Balaam bade Balak stand by his burnt offering while he went to meet the Lord yonder, and that the Lord met him and put a word in his mouth.

debates: Why Balak changed the place: Clarke and Wesley suppose the first sight had intimidated Balaam or raised his admiration, Henry doubles the alternative and adds a plan of attacking the quarter then in view, and Calvin explains it from the art itself, that enchanters were commonly believed to work by the gaze

What the clause about seeing the utmost part means: Ellicott makes it turn on the disputed interpretation of the earlier verse and sets out both consequences without choosing, while Calvin reports the same ambiguity and, through his editor, Marckius's judgement that the Hebrew tense needs no alteration

Where the field of Zophim was: Gill takes the name from a watch tower and reports Jarchi's picture of a watchman posted against armies, while Ellicott identifies the spot with the height from which Moses afterwards surveyed the land, allowing that Pisgah may have had several summits

What Balak's renewed question shows: Calvin makes it the hypocrite's anxious inquiry after a will he finds intolerable, while Clarke makes it a real concession that Balaam was wholly under Jehovah's influence, coupled with the hope that God might change his mind
Who was still present at the second sacrifice: Gill reports from Jarchi that the earlier all the princes of Moab is not repeated here, some having withdrawn when they saw there was no hope
outliers: Calvin's report from profane writers that the gaze of the enchanter was believed to have much effect upon his art
Ellicott's willingness to set out two opposite senses of the verse and leave the choice with the reader
The editorial note in Calvin's block reporting Marckius on the Hebrew tense
Henry's image of the fireballs of Balaam's curses aimed at the quarter of the camp then in view
Henry's wish that we were as earnest to obtain the blessing as Balak was to procure a curse
Gill's observation, from Jarchi, that the princes of Moab thinned out between the first attempt and the second
Ellicott's note that Balak himself speaks of God under the name Jehovah

18.pericope_label: God who does not repent, and the iniquity not beheld in Jacob

schools.summary: Gill says the parable was the word put into Balaam's mouth and pronounced. On the declaration that God is not a man he argues from the nature of God: man is a creature consisting of a body of flesh and blood and of a created and finite soul, but God, though the parts of a human body are ascribed to him in a figurative sense, is not to be conceived of in a corporeal manner, and though he is a Spirit he is eternal, immense and infinite; much less is he as sinful man, who goes astray from the womb speaking lies. Let God be true and every man a liar: he is God that cannot lie, his counsels of old are faithfulness and truth, his promises yea and amen in Christ, and the prophecies of Scripture are punctually accomplished, particularly what he foretold of the people of Israel and promised to them, that they should be happy and inherit the land of Canaan; there could be no hope by any means whatever of making him false and unfaithful to his word. The commandment to bless he takes of a charge to pronounce a blessing upon Israel and to declare them a happy people. On the iniquity not beheld he says it is not that there was no sin in them, nor any observed by the Lord, but that he did not mark it in strict justice and punish for it, forgiving it, hiding his face from it, and not imputing it to them. Calvin says the expression about taking up a parable means to make use of glowing and elevated language in order the more to awaken the attention of the hearer, and that the preface calling on Balak to rise up and hear has the same object. Of the commandment to bless he says a command had been given and a positive law laid down for Balaam, since he was not free and independent in this matter but God had bound him to exercise the prophetic office even against his own will, so that he declares it is not in his power to alter it. On the iniquity not beheld he reports that some understand the two words of idols, which bring nothing but deadly labour and trouble to their worshippers, as if it were said that Israel was pure and untainted by such offences in duly serving the one true God; but how will it be correct to say that God saw no idolatry in the people, when they had so openly fallen into it, since although the golden calf was made only once their manifold and almost constant rebellions forbid these wicked and perverse men from being thus absolved. Since the two words in connection signify all sorts of iniquities which tend to men's hurt, a more proper meaning will be that such iniquity is not seen in Jacob as to include him with the nations that are given to violence and crime; yet even so the former question still arises, for we know that the Israelites were scarcely better than the worst of mankind. Some reply feebly, he says, that it was not seen because God did not impute it; but in his opinion nothing else is meant by these words than that the people were pleasing to God because he had sanctified them. If any object that they were not therefore any the more just or innocent, the answer is easy, that it is not here declared what they were, but only God's grace is magnified, who deigned to exalt them as a holy nation; in this way Jerusalem was the holy city and the royal abode of God though it was a den of thieves, and on this ground Paul says that the children of Abraham were holy branches because they sprang from a holy root, and in the same sense they are everywhere called God's children however degenerate they might be. God is therefore said to have seen no iniquity in them with reference to his adoption.

Clarke says the declaration that God is not a man that he should lie seems to be spoken to correct the foregoing supposition of Balak that God could change his mind, and observes that even the heathen would not allow that their supreme god could be caught in a falsity, quoting Aeschylus for the sentiment. The saying that God has not beheld iniquity in Jacob he calls a difficult passage: if we take the words as spoken of the people Israel, their iniquity and perverseness were almost unparalleled and such words cannot be spoken of them with strict truth, but if we consider them as spoken of the patriarch Jacob, or of Jacob after he became Israel, they are most strictly true, since after that time a more unblemished and noble character, Abraham excepted, is not to be found in the page of history, whether sacred or profane, and for his sake, and for his father Isaac's and his grandfather Abraham's, God is ever represented as favouring, blessing and sparing a rebellious and undeserving people; in this way, he thinks, the difficult text may be safely understood. There is another way, he adds, which will give a good sense: the first Hebrew word not only signifies iniquity but most frequently trouble, labour, distress and affliction, these being indeed its ideal meanings, iniquity being only an accommodated or metaphorical one because of the pain that sin produces; and the second word, which occurs often in Scripture, is never translated perverseness except in this place, signifying simply labour, especially of an afflictive or oppressive kind, so that the words may be considered as implying that God will not suffer the people to be oppressed. Wesley glosses the two verbs of the nineteenth verse, that to lie would be to break the promises made to his people for their preservation and benediction, and to repent would be to change his counsels or purposes, unless he see iniquity in Jacob; and the iniquity of the following verse he takes as not such as was in the Canaanites, such as God will punish with a curse and utter destruction. That the Lord is with him means that he has a favour for this people and will defend and save them, and the shout of a king means such joyful and triumphant shouts as those with which a people congratulate their sovereign. The summons to rise up he takes as implying the diligent attention required, that Balak should rouse up himself and carefully mind what was said.

Keil's blocks on this span are chiefly verse quotation, recording that Balaam meets Balak's expectation that he will take back the blessing he has uttered with the declaration that he cannot turn it, and that after this decided reversal of Balak's expectations he carried out still more fully the blessing which had been only briefly indicated. Ellicott observes that the adoption of the words about God not being a son of man that he should repent, with slight variation, by Samuel affords evidence of his familiarity with this portion of the Pentateuch. On the saying about iniquity he notes that the same combination of the two Hebrew words, the one meaning iniquity or injustice and the other perverseness, or rather suffering or grievance, occurs in Habakkuk; and that the word rendered shout is the same which occurs in Leviticus of the trumpet blast.

debates: What it means that God beheld no iniquity in Jacob: Gill takes it of non-imputation, Wesley narrows the word to iniquity of the Canaanite sort deserving utter destruction, Clarke refers the words to the patriarch rather than the nation or else takes the Hebrew in its commoner sense of affliction, and Calvin rejects the non-imputation answer as feeble and grounds the saying in God's adoption and sanctifying grace
Whether the two Hebrew words mean idols: Calvin reports the reading and refuses it, since Israel had openly fallen into idolatry and their almost constant rebellions forbid such an absolution

Whether the words can be spoken of Israel at all with strict truth: Clarke says they cannot and transfers them to Jacob personally, while Calvin keeps them of the nation and answers that what is declared is not what the people were but the grace that exalted them as a holy nation

What lying and repenting would mean in God: Gill argues from the divine nature against a corporeal or mutable conception, Clarke takes the line as a correction of Balak's assumption, and Wesley defines lying as breaking promises and repenting as changing counsels
Why Balaam cannot retract: Calvin says a positive law was laid on him and he was bound to the prophetic office even against his will, while Keil states simply that he cannot turn the blessing
outliers: Calvin's dismissal of the non-imputation answer as a feeble reply, which is the very answer Gill gives
Calvin's parallels that Jerusalem was the holy city while it was a den of thieves, and that Abraham's children are holy branches from a holy root
Clarke's philological escape route, that the words for iniquity and perverseness more commonly mean trouble and afflictive labour
Clarke's judgement that after Jacob became Israel a nobler character, Abraham excepted, is not to be found in sacred or profane history
Clarke's citation of Aeschylus, that even the heathen would not allow their supreme god to be caught in a falsity
Ellicott's use of Samuel's echo of this verse as evidence of his familiarity with the Pentateuch
Gill's insistence that the human parts ascribed to God are figurative, against a corporeal conception

22.pericope_label: The strength of the wild ox, the failure of enchantment, and the lion

schools.summary: Gill says God brought them out of Egypt with a mighty hand and stretched out arm, and will conduct them through the wilderness and bring them safe to Canaan, so that he who brought them thence will not suffer them to perish by any means and it is vain to attempt to curse such a people. On the denial of enchantment he says Balaam here owns that all his enchantments and divinations signified nothing and would never prevail to bring a curse upon Israel, so that it was a vain thing for him to use them. The great lion he prefers to render the lioness, which, as Aelian says, is the strongest and most warlike beast, the most fierce and furious, as is believed both by Greeks and barbarians, and he mentions the heroism of Perdiccas the Macedonian. Calvin says the bringing out of Egypt assigns a reason for their constant success, because God, having once redeemed this people, will not forsake the work which he has begun, the argument being drawn from the continued course of God's blessings, which, since they flow from an inexhaustible fountain, are of infinite progress. On the denial of enchantment he reports three interpretations: the passage is commonly expounded as an encomium on the people, because they are not given to enchantments and magical superstitions, as God had strictly enjoined in his law that they should not pollute themselves by such defilements; others explain it that the Israelites shall not want enchanters, because by the Urim and Thummim, or by the prophets, God would reveal to them whatever should be profitable; but their opinion is more correct who interpret it that no enchantment and no divination avails against the Israelites. In his own judgment Balaam confesses that there is no room for his enchantments, or that his customary arts fail him now, because their efficacy and power cannot affect the Israelites; and this confession harmonizes with the words of Pharaoh's magicians when they said, this is the finger of God, after they had pertinaciously contended until God compelled them to yield. Thus Balaam declares that the elect people were defended from on high, so that his divinations were ineffectual and his enchantments vain; and the other clause he takes simply to mean that God would henceforth perform mighty works for the defence of his people. Of the lion he enters a caution, that the comparison is not in every respect accurate, since it does not signify that the Israelites should be cruel or rapacious, but merely bold and strong and prompt in their resistance if any should provoke them.

Clarke argues at length about the horned beast. It is generally allowed, he says, that there is no such beast in nature as the unicorn, that is, a creature of the horse kind with one long rich curled horn in the forehead, the creature painted from fancy being represented as one of the supporters of the royal arms of Great Britain; it is difficult to say what kind of beast is intended by the original word, the Septuagint translating it the one-horned animal and the Vulgate sometimes unicorn and in this text rhinoceros. That no single-horned animal can be intended by the reem of Moses is sufficiently evident from this, that Moses, speaking of Joseph, says he has the horns of a reem, where the horns are spoken of in the plural and the animal in the singular; the creature referred to is therefore either the rhinoceros, some varieties of which have two horns on the nose, or the wild bull, urus or buffalo, though some think the beast intended is a species of goat, but the rhinoceros seems to him the most likely. On the denial of enchantment he says that because God has determined to save them, therefore no enchantment can prevail against them, and he would read the following clause as, at this time it shall be told to Jacob and to Israel what God worketh. The great lion he takes as the great, mighty or old lion, the king of the forest, who is feared and respected by all the other beasts of the field, so that Israel shall be the subduer and possessor of the whole land of Canaan. Wesley says the bringing out of Egypt was by a strong hand and in spite of all their enemies, so that it is in vain to seek or hope to overcome them, and explains the change from plural to singular as very common in the Hebrew language. On the denial of enchantment he adds that it holds against any that truly believe in Christ, and exclaims how wonderful and glorious are the works which God is now about to do for Israel, which will be a matter of discourse and admiration to all ages. The lion he takes of action, that as a lion rouses up himself to fight or to go out to the prey, so shall Israel stir up themselves to warlike attempts against their enemies and not rest or cease from fighting and pursuing.

Keil renders the clause about Egypt as God bringing them out, noting that the participle is not used for the preterite but designates the leading, and takes the word for the horned beast as the buffalo, its strength being like that of a buffalo. On the denial of enchantment he grounds it in the fellowship of its God in which Israel rejoiced and to which it owed its strength, and on the closing figure he says that through the power of its God Israel was invincible and would crush all its foes. Ellicott renders the clause about Egypt literally as, is bringing them, the use of the participle denoting the continuance of the action, since he who brought them forth out of Egypt was still conducting them on their march, and finds an obvious allusion in these words to those of Balak earlier. The denial of enchantment he renders as, for there is no augury in Jacob, and there is no divination in Israel; at the set time it is told to Jacob and to Israel what God hath done. The ordinary meanings of the two Hebrew words, the use of the same preposition as in the previous verse, and especially the second clause of the verse seem to him to decide the sense: the Israelites had no need of augury and divination, seeing that God revealed to them his acts, his counsel and his will. He quotes Hengstenberg, that what is here affirmed of Israel applies to the Church of all ages and also to every individual believer, since the Church of God knows from his own Word what God does and what it has to do in consequence, whereas the wisdom of this world resembles augury and divination. The great lion he renders better as a lioness, and observes that Balaam transfers to the whole nation that which Jacob had prophesied of Judah.

debates: What the denial of enchantment means: Calvin reports three readings, that Israel does not practise divination, that Israel has no need of diviners since God reveals by Urim and prophets, and that no divination avails against Israel, and prefers the third, taking Balaam to confess that his own arts have failed; Ellicott adopts the first and grounds it in Israel's having no need of augury, while Clarke and Gill take the third

What beast the horned creature is: Clarke denies that any single-horned animal can be meant, since Moses gives the reem plural horns, and settles on the rhinoceros or the wild bull, while Keil renders it buffalo without argument

What the participle about Egypt implies: Ellicott and Keil agree that it denotes continuing action rather than a past deliverance, and Calvin draws from it that God will not forsake the work he has begun, the blessings flowing from an inexhaustible fountain

Whether the lion figure is exact: Calvin enters a caution that it does not make the Israelites cruel or rapacious but only bold and prompt in resistance, while Clarke makes Israel the subduer and possessor of Canaan and Wesley reads it of stirring up to warlike attempts
Whether the beast is lion or lioness: Ellicott and Gill both prefer the lioness, Ellicott adding that Balaam transfers to the whole nation what Jacob had prophesied of Judah alone
outliers: Clarke's observation that the fanciful unicorn survives as a supporter of the royal arms of Great Britain
Calvin's parallel between Balaam's confession and the words of Pharaoh's magicians, this is the finger of God
Ellicott's quotation of Hengstenberg, that the wisdom of this world resembles augury while the Church knows from God's Word what God does
Gill's citation of Aelian on the lioness as the most warlike beast, and of the heroism of Perdiccas the Macedonian
Calvin's image of blessings flowing from an inexhaustible fountain and therefore of infinite progress
Wesley's note that the change from plural to singular is very common in Hebrew
Ellicott's argument from the preposition, which decides his rendering of the enchantment clause

25.pericope_label: Balak’s exasperation and the third station on the top of Peor

schools.summary: Gill says Balak's words signify that it would be as well or better to do nothing at all than to do what Balaam did, but that the sense is not that he would not have him curse them, since that was what he could not bear to lose. Of Balaam's reply he says he appeals to Balak for his honesty and faithfulness, for honest and faithful he would be thought to be, both to God and man, since when they first met he plainly told him what he must expect. The third proposal he explains as a change to a place which, if not better for the view of the people, was yet a more religious place, on which account the king hoped for success; and he says Balaam was willing to try again, to gratify the king, and especially to get the wages of unrighteousness, which he dearly loved, as the apostle says. Peor he calls the name of a high mountain in Moab, so called from a gap or opening in it, where the idol Baal was worshipped and from which he had the name of Baal-peor, and where very probably there was a temple. Of the last sacrifices he notes that though they were expensive Balak did not grudge them, sparing no cost to gain his point, though he could now have but little hope of it. Calvin says that here we may behold as in a mirror how wretchedly unbelievers are driven to and fro, so as to alternate between vain hopes and fears, though by their changes of purpose they are still brought back to the same errors, as if their blind passion carried them round in a circle. Of Balaam's answer he says the mercenary prophet here confesses that he has no more power of himself to be silent than to speak, and that there is no doubt he would excuse himself with servility to the proud king, to whom he would willingly have sold himself.

Clarke says the top of Peor was probably the place where the famous Baal-peor had his chief temple, and that this deity appears to have been the Priapus of the Moabites, worshipped with the same obscene and abominable rites. Wesley calls Peor a high place named Beth-peor, that is, the house or temple of Peor, so called because there they worshipped Baal-peor.

Keil records that Balak was not deterred from making another attempt, exclaiming at first in indignation that Balaam should neither curse them at all nor bless them at all, and that Balaam answered by appealing to what he had told him already, that all the Lord speaks, that he must do. Of the last preparation he notes that the sacrifices offered for this fresh transaction were the same as in the former cases, and that Balak did as Balaam had said, offering a bullock and a ram on every altar. Ellicott observes that Balak here makes mention of God as Elohim, and that he appears to be satisfied that Balaam was hindered by God from uttering the curses which he desired him to pronounce upon Israel. Mount Peor he describes as one peak of the northern part of the mountains of Abarim, nearer than the other heights to the camp of the Israelites, looking toward or over the face of Jeshimon, that is, the waste or desert.

debates: What Balak means by neither curse nor bless: Gill takes it as exasperation rather than instruction, since the curse was the one thing he wanted, Keil calls it an exclamation of indignation, and Calvin makes it a specimen of the unbeliever driven to and fro between vain hopes and fears

What Balaam's reply amounts to: Calvin makes it the confession of a mercenary who has no more power to be silent than to speak and would gladly have sold himself to the king, while Gill hears in it a claim to honesty and faithfulness towards God and man alike

Why the third station was chosen: Gill says it was not for a better view but because the place was more religious, which distinguishes this move from the second, and Ellicott notes that Balak now speaks of God as Elohim where he had earlier used the name Jehovah

What Peor was: Gill derives the name from a gap or opening in the mountain, Clarke and Wesley identify it as the seat of Baal-peor's chief temple, Clarke adding that the deity was the Priapus of the Moabites worshipped with obscene rites, while Ellicott gives only its position among the mountains of Abarim
Why Balaam agreed to another attempt: Gill says he wished to gratify the king and especially to get the wages of unrighteousness, which he dearly loved
outliers: Calvin's mirror, in which the unbeliever's changes of purpose bring him back to the same errors
Calvin's judgement that Balaam would willingly have sold himself to the proud king
Clarke's identification of Baal-peor with the Priapus of the Moabites and his obscene rites
Gill's derivation of the name Peor from a gap or opening in the mountain
Ellicott's note that Balak's name for God shifts to Elohim at this point
Gill's remark that Balak spared no cost though he could now have but little hope
Ellicott's topographical detail that Peor looked over the face of Jeshimon, the waste
